lessons.title: Memory and I/O at a glance: vmstat and free
lessons.goal:
Read every column of `vmstat`, watch memory, swap and disk I/O change while a file is written, and learn which numbers matter.

Why it matters: `vmstat 1` is the quickest way to see CPU, memory, swap and I/O together. One screen of it often answers "is it CPU, memory or disk?"

setup.note: Steps write a few hundred MB of temporary files with `dd` in /tmp/lab and delete them. Needs sysstat (`dnf install sysstat`).

steps.title: The columns
steps.text:
`vmstat 1` prints a line per second:

- **procs**: `r` runnable, `b` blocked in uninterruptible sleep.
- **memory** (KB): `swpd` swap used, `free`, `buff` (block cache), `cache` (page cache).
- **swap**: `si` pages swapped in, `so` swapped out, per second.
- **io**: `bi` blocks read from devices, `bo` blocks written, per second.
- **system**: `in` interrupts, `cs` context switches.
- **cpu**: `us sy id wa st`.

The first line is the average since boot.

run.output:
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
 1  0 1240528  94588      0 2141392   34   33  7139    95    3    3  6  3 81  7  2

steps.title: free in context
steps.text: `free -m` shows RAM and swap in MB. `available` is the estimate of memory usable by new programs without swapping.

run.output:
total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            5642        3655         102          30        2091        1987
Swap:           4095        1211        2884

steps.title: Watch I/O while writing a file
steps.text: We write 300 MB with direct I/O (bypassing the page cache) in the background and sample `vmstat` for four seconds. `bo` (blocks out) and `b` rise while the disk works; the CPU shows `wa`.

run.cmd: dd if=/dev/zero of=big.dat bs=1M count=300 oflag=direct status=none & D=$!; vmstat 1 4 | awk 'NR==2 {print "b bo wa"} NR>3 {print $2, $10, $16}'; wait $D

steps.after: The first sample (the since-boot average) is skipped. While `dd` runs `bo` is large; afterwards it falls back to nearly zero.

steps.title: Cached writes versus direct writes
steps.text: Without `oflag=direct` the data first goes into the page cache and the disk write happens later: `dd` reports a very high speed, and the **dirty** counters grow. `vmstat` shows `bo` after the fact.

run.cmd: dd if=/dev/zero of=cached.dat bs=1M count=300 2>&1 | tail -n 1 | awk '{print "cached write speed:", $(NF-1), $NF}'; grep -E '^Dirty:' /proc/meminfo | awk '{print "dirty pages now:", $2, "kB"}'
run.output:
cached write speed: 338 MB/s
dirty pages now: 282796 kB

run.cmd: sync; grep -E '^Dirty:' /proc/meminfo | awk '{print "after sync:", $2, "kB"}'; rm -f big.dat cached.dat

steps.under: `vmstat` reads `/proc/stat`, `/proc/meminfo` and `/proc/vmstat` twice and subtracts. `bi`/`bo` are in 1 KB blocks. The page cache hides disk speed from programs: benchmark with `oflag=direct` or `fio`, and look at `iostat` for the real device.

quiz.q: What does the `b` column of vmstat show?

quiz.explain: Pages swapped in and out per second.

quiz.q: Why is `dd` without oflag=direct so fast?
options: It writes into the page cache; the disk write happens later
It is the average since boot, not the current rate
quiz.explain: Only later lines show the sampled interval.

check.scenario: `vmstat 1` shows `si`/`so` of 2000 pages per second and `wa` 40% while `free` shows 100 MB available. What is happening and what do you do first?
check.answer: The system is **swapping heavily** (memory saturation) and stalling on swap I/O. Find the consumers (`ps aux --sort=-rss | head`, `smem`), check for a leak or too many workers, reduce memory use or add RAM; as a stopgap tune `vm.swappiness` and add a cgroup limit to the greediest service. Check `dmesg` for OOM kills.

lessons.title: Disk and network statistics: iostat, pidstat -d, sar
lessons.goal:
Measure a disk precisely with `iostat -x`, attribute I/O to processes with `pidstat -d`, and use `sar` for live and historical numbers.

Why it matters: "the disk is slow" needs numbers: throughput, IOPS, latency and queue depth. These tools produce them and show who is responsible.

setup.note: Steps write a few hundred MB of temporary files with `dd` in /tmp/lab and delete them. Needs sysstat (`dnf install sysstat`).

steps.title: iostat -x: the key columns
steps.text: `iostat -dx 1` per device: `r/s`, `w/s` (IOPS), `rkB/s`, `wkB/s` (throughput), `r_await`, `w_await` (average latency in ms: queue plus service time), `aqu-sz` (average queue length) and `%util` (share of time the device had requests in flight). We write with direct I/O and sample the disk.

run.cmd: dd if=/dev/zero of=io.dat bs=1M count=300 oflag=direct status=none & D=$!; sleep 0.5; iostat -dx 1 2 sda | awk '$1=="sda" {w=$8; k=$9; a=$12; q=$(NF-1); u=$NF} END {print "device w/s wkB/s w_await aqu-sz %util"; print "sda", w, k, a, q, u}'; wait $D
run.output:
[1] 380953
device w/s wkB/s w_await aqu-sz %util
sda 40.59 16265.35 51.83 140.72 88.71

steps.title: Who is doing the I/O: pidstat -d
steps.text: `pidstat -d 1` reports kB read and written per second **per process**. Here only `dd` writes.

run.cmd: dd if=/dev/zero of=io.dat bs=1M count=300 oflag=direct status=none & D=$!; sleep 0.5; pidstat -d -p $D 1 2 | awk '/Average/ {print "dd: kB_rd/s", $4, "kB_wr/s", $5}'; wait $D; rm -f io.dat

run.reason: iotop is not installed on this machine; pidstat -d shows the same per-process numbers

steps.title: sar: live
steps.text: `sar` (from sysstat) samples many counters: `-u` CPU, `-r` memory, `-b` I/O totals, `-n DEV` network. With an interval it reports live, like `vmstat`.

steps.title: sar: history
steps.text: A systemd timer (`sysstat-collect.timer`) stores samples every 10 minutes in `/var/log/sa/saDD`, so you can ask *yesterday* questions with `sar -u -f FILE` or `sar -s 02:00 -e 03:00`. That is what makes sysstat valuable after the incident.

run.cmd: ls /var/log/sa 2>/dev/null | head -n 1 | wc -l | awk '{print ($1 > 0) ? "history files exist" : "no history yet: the collector has not run on this machine"}'
run.output: no history yet: the collector has not run on this machine

steps.under: All these tools read the same kernel counters: `/proc/diskstats` (reads, writes, sectors, time in I/O, weighted time in queue per device) and `/proc/net/dev`. `iostat` computes rates and derived values from two snapshots. `%util` is the fraction of the interval during which the device had at least one request, so for devices that handle many requests in parallel (SSD, NVMe, arrays) 100% does not mean saturated: look at `aqu-sz` and `await`.

quiz.q: What does iostat's `%util` of 100% mean for an NVMe SSD?
options: Not necessarily: it only says a request was always in flight
quiz.explain: Parallel devices need aqu-sz and await to judge.

quiz.q: Which tool attributes disk I/O to processes?
What stores sar history on this system?

options: Average time per request including queueing, in ms

check.scenario: Users report that reports run slowly between 02:00 and 03:00 last night. Which tool lets you check the disk and CPU for that window, and what must be in place?
check.answer: `sar -u -s 02:00:00 -e 03:00:00 -f /var/log/sa/saDD` (and `-d` for disks, `-r` memory, `-q` load), which requires the sysstat collector (`sysstat-collect.timer`) to have been running. Without history you can only guess; consider shipping metrics to a time-series system (Prometheus/Grafana).

interview.q: What are the most useful vmstat columns?
interview.a: r and b (processes), si/so (swapping), bi/bo (I/O), us/sy/id/wa/st (CPU). See [the lesson](#/lesson/43/vmstat-free).

interview.q: How do you tell whether the disk is the bottleneck?
interview.a: `iostat -x`: high await and growing aqu-sz with high %util (on a single disk), or high wa in vmstat with tasks in D state. See [the lesson](#/lesson/43/iostat-pidstat-sar).

interview.q: Why is free memory not the right number to watch?
interview.a: The kernel uses free RAM for the page cache. `available` (free plus reclaimable) and swap activity are the right indicators.

interview.q: How do you find which process generates disk I/O?
What is the difference between buffered and direct I/O?
interview.a: Buffered I/O goes through the page cache and is written later; direct I/O (O_DIRECT) bypasses the cache and shows the device's real speed.

interview.q: What does sar add to the other tools?
interview.a: History: it records counters periodically so you can analyse past periods.

glossary.def: Command showing processes, memory, swap, I/O and CPU per interval.
The number of I/O requests waiting or in service (aqu-sz).
System Activity Reporter from sysstat: live and historical counters.
I/O that bypasses the page cache (O_DIRECT).

commands.desc: Five one-second samples of system state.
